translations: Lan Caihe swallowed the compliment and quickly changed the subject: “Your moves are so smooth, even the sea follows you out.”
Lü Dongbin turned around and said, “If you’re jealous, just borrow the flower basket later and give the sea a good wash.”

He stopped dreaming of slicing the East Sea in half from shore to shore. He only opened a path wide enough for himself right in front of him. With each crash of a wave, he thrust another sword. Every flash of his blade dealt only with the obstacle right before him, leaving the distant gourds and wind‑fans untouched.

When the paper donkey accidentally drifted into his sword path, Lü Dongbin halted his blade and let it pass, rather than tearing a bigger gap in the water. Zhang Guolao, hearing the drum’s echo turn to silence, would also pat the donkey to steer it clear of the sword light. Their words still sparred, but neither let the other’s skill become a roadblock.
Hearing the splash behind him, Zhang Guolao tapped his fishing drum and asked, “Who’s catching up?”
Lü Dongbin replied, “Someone walking forward, face to the front.”
“That’s a pity. You can only see the place you haven’t reached yet, not how far you’ve already walked.”
“You, on the other hand, see everything—except the next wave.”

The two kept crossing the sea, one ahead of the other. The paper donkey rode the waves, the fishing drum marked the rhythm; the treasured sword split the surf, and Lü Dongbin rode his sword. Neither copied the other’s method, nor finished the other’s journey for them.

Only four immortals remained on the shore, yet to set out. He Xiangu watched the two routes on the sea, gently turning the lotus she held. When Lan Caihe stepped forward, she lifted her flower basket, saying, “This time, it’s finally the flowers’ turn.”

He Xiangu placed the lotus on the water. The petals unfurled in the wind, forming a steady little platform. She stepped onto the lotus, clutching its stem, and drifted slowly away from shore on the first wave.

Lan Caihe also set his flower basket down into the sea. It floated nicely, but the blossoms inside refused to stay still—every gust made them stretch out in every direction. Lan Caihe stepped onto the basket’s rim, proudly waving to the shore, “My path can still blossom.”

No sooner had he spoken than a stray flower stem snagged He Xiangu’s lotus leaf. The lotus hesitated, while the basket kept drifting forward; the two magical tools tugged each other, and neither could move smoothly.
He Xiangu turned back and asked, “Are you crossing the sea, or just coming to pick my flowers?”
Lan Caihe hurried to untangle the stem, “Traveling together, traveling together. The flowers are just a bit more enthusiastic than I am.”
“Then ask them to tuck that enthusiasm back into the basket.”

Lan Caihe gathered the over‑reaching stems back together. Freed from the tug, the basket slipped forward with the waves again. He Xiangu didn’t wait for the water to calm; she gently twisted the lotus stem, letting the flower steer with each crest. When a wave hit from the side, the leaf tilted aside; when a wave rose from ahead, the petals lifted her up, then set her down steadily.
Seeing her glide so smoothly, Lan Caihe said, “If I’d known, I’d have brought a lotus myself.”
He Xiangu replied, “Just keep that basket under control. Adding another flower might make the East Sea bloom into a shop.”

A sudden surge tossed the flower basket sideways. Lan Caihe thought about grabbing the lotus stem, remembered his earlier clumsiness, and instead retracted his hand, using the basket’s handle to paddle. The basket turned slowly but gradually steered back to run parallel with the lotus.
He Xiangu didn’t pull him along; she simply described the upcoming surf: “Left side’s breaking waves, right side’s long rollers. Which do you choose?”
“Left,” he answered. “If the breaking waves bully you, at least they line up in a queue.”

They pressed forward, one to the left, one to the right. The lotus supported her, the basket floated on the sea; their routes looked alike but their temperaments were completely different. He Xiangu rode the waves, unlike the East Sea’s stubborn push; Lan Caihe negotiated with every flower stem, telling them not to make friends with other travelers’ tools.

Suddenly a chaotic surge erupted ahead, scattering the lotus and the basket apart. He Xiangu didn’t chase the basket; she shouted to Lan Caihe, “Don’t try to wrestle the wave!” She slipped with the current, looped around, then turned back from a calmer patch. Lan Caihe did the same; his basket took a longer detour but didn’t snag the lotus leaf again.
“So taking a roundabout still counts as moving forward,” Lan Caihe said.
“As long as you don’t end up back on shore.”
“That’s the path Iron Crutch Li used before; I won’t steal it.”
From afar, Iron Crutch Li, perched on the sea, shouted, “Did everyone behind you catch up?”
He Xiangu answered, “They did. It’s just that Lan Caihe’s flowers are busier than people.”
Lan Caihe immediately defended his basket, “It’s their first time crossing the sea; they haven’t seen much yet.”
Zhang Guolao, with his back to the group, laughed, “Don’t worry, after this they’ll be able to blow backwards too.”

He Xiangu and Lan Caihe finally caught up with the four ahead. At last, all six immortals had used their own powers to enter the East Sea; He Xiangu was never left on the shore, nor did anyone else finish the crossing for her.
